# Frontier Sector Code — General Part
## Part I — General Provisions
### Article 1 — Jurisdiction
1.1. This Code applies throughout the Frontier Sector, including all stations, outposts, ships, vessels, derelicts, expedition sites, and other facilities.
1.2. Every person present in the Sector is subject to this Code and entitled to its protections.
1.3. The Code applies to SolGov citizens, residents, visitors, corporate employees, foreign nationals, and members of hostile or illegal organizations.
### Article 2 — Equality Before the Law
2.1. Every person is equal before the law. No rank, office, wealth, species, employer, or faction grants immunity.
2.2. Any exception to a law must be expressly stated in that law.
2.3. Public officials may exercise lawful authority, but they remain subject to the Code.
2.4. An order does not excuse an obviously unlawful act. The person who issues an unlawful order bears primary responsibility; a person who knowingly carries out an obviously unlawful act is also liable.
2.5. The Code is written as a system of perfect legality. In practice, SolGov officials may claim exemptions or influence; such conduct is not law and may itself be an offense.
### Article 3 — Definitions
3.1. [bold]Person[/bold] means a sapient being, including humans and other sapient species, and Synths.
3.2. [bold]Sapient[/bold] means capable of reason, self-awareness, and moral judgment.
3.3. [bold]Silicon[/bold] means a lawed artificial being or robot. A Silicon is not a person for purposes of criminal liability unless it is a Synth.
3.4. [bold]Vessel[/bold] means any ship, shuttle, station, outpost, or structure capable of independent operation.
3.5. [bold]Public place[/bold] means any SolGov-administered station, outpost, or point of interest open to the public, including Frontier Outpost, Trade Mall, NFSD Outpost, Medical Dispatch, Edison, and Expeditionary Lodge, and the public areas of any other station or outpost.
3.6. [bold]Private place[/bold] means private quarters, dormitories, bathrooms, private vessels, closed businesses, and other spaces not open to the public.
3.7. [bold]Contraband[/bold] means an item restricted by this Code, the Penal Code, or a schedule adopted under them.
3.8. [bold]Probable cause[/bold] means facts that would lead a reasonable officer to believe that an offense has been, is being, or is about to be committed.
3.9. [bold]Deed[/bold] means a registered document establishing ownership of a vessel.
3.10. [bold]Salvage[/bold] means the lawful recovery of abandoned, derelict, or unregistered property or vessels.
3.11. [bold]Lethal force[/bold] means force likely to cause death or serious bodily injury.
### Article 4 — Culpability and Liability
4.1. A person may be liable for an offense committed intentionally, knowingly, recklessly, or with criminal negligence, as the offense requires.
4.2. [bold]Attempt[/bold] requires intent to commit an offense and a substantial step toward committing it.
4.3. [bold]Complicity[/bold] requires intentionally aiding, abetting, or procuring an offense. Mere presence or association is not enough.
4.4. [bold]Conspiracy[/bold] requires an agreement to commit an offense and an overt act in furtherance of it.
4.5. Ignorance of the law is not a defense. Mistake of fact may negate intent where it is reasonable and genuine.
4.6. A person acting under unlawful mind control is not culpable if they lacked control over their actions. The controller and anyone who knowingly enabled the control are liable.
4.7. A corporation may be liable as a legal person. Its directing officers may also be personally liable.
### Article 5 — Private Rules and Contracts
5.1. A vessel’s captain or owner may set reasonable rules for access to, and use of, that vessel.
5.2. Vessel rules are private terms, not criminal law. They cannot authorize an offense, override this Code, or compel an unlawful act.
5.3. A person may accept or decline a vessel’s terms. A captain may deny access to a person who declines. A person aboard may decline the terms and leave, subject to immediate safety needs.
5.4. A captain may permit nudity aboard their private vessel. A captain may not compel a person to undress or to remain aboard against their will.
5.5. Contracts and agreements cannot waive basic rights or nullify the Code. An unlawful term is void.
5.6. Anyone who enters a vessel is deemed to have accepted the captain’s rules. The rules remain subject to this Code and cannot authorize an offense.
## Part II — Rights and Liberties
### Article 6 — Protected Rights
6.1. The following rights are protected in the Frontier Sector:
- freedom of speech and expression; - freedom of the press; - peaceful assembly and protest; - freedom of religion and conscience; - freedom of movement; - privacy in private places; - property rights; - fair treatment before the law.
6.2. These rights are not absolute. They may be restricted only by a law reasonably related to public safety, public order, or the rights of others.
6.3. Slavery and involuntary servitude are prohibited. Lawful confinement and community service are not slavery.
6.4. No person may be subjected to torture, collective punishment, or punishment of their family or associates for their own conduct.
### Article 7 — Speech
7.1. Speech is protected unless it falls within a defined offense.
7.2. The following are offenses:
- a credible threat of violence; - incitement to imminent violence; - defamation; - a false emergency or distress report; - sedition, as defined in Article 42; - disclosure of classified SolGov information; - targeted harassment, as defined in Article 21.
7.3. Criticism of SolGov, the NFSD, or public officials is not, by itself, an offense.
### Article 8 — Assembly and Protest
8.1. Peaceful assembly and protest are lawful without a permit.
8.2. Assembly becomes unlawful when it:
- blocks access to a public service or emergency route; - occupies a restricted area; - causes property damage; - involves violence or the threat of violence; - continues after a lawful dispersal order.
8.3. Property damage, violence, obstruction, and refusal to disperse are separately chargeable offenses.
### Article 9 — Religion
9.1. Freedom of religion and conscience is protected.
9.2. Religious practice does not excuse an offense. Human sacrifice, forced conversion, blood-cult violence, and similar harmful practices are crimes.
9.3. A chaplain may officiate, counsel, and visit prisoners, subject to reasonable security restrictions.
### Article 10 — Privacy and Surveillance
10.1. Private places are protected from unreasonable search and surveillance.
10.2. A search of a private place requires a warrant, consent, or a recognized exception under Article 15.
10.3. Medical records, personal data, and private communications are protected. Disclosure requires consent, a warrant, or a public-safety exception.
10.4. A vessel’s captain or owner may monitor their own vessel and may consent to searches of it.
10.5. Evidence obtained through an unlawful search may be excluded by a tribunal.
### Article 11 — Emergency Powers
11.1. The Station Representative or the Sheriff may declare a state of emergency, curfew, or quarantine for public safety. Central Command may extend or revoke it.
11.2. The declaring authority sets the duration and may renew it. A declaration may be challenged before a tribunal, but it is not suspended solely by a private party.
11.3. Emergency powers may include restricting movement, closing areas, imposing a curfew, requiring evacuation, and authorizing inspections.
11.4. Emergency powers may not suspend medical care, the right to counsel, or the right to challenge detention. They may not authorize torture or collective punishment.
11.5. Final review of an emergency declaration belongs to Central Command and SolGov officials.
## Part III — Courts, Warrants, and Detention
### Article 12 — Judicial Authority
12.1. Sentences are carried by the highest available authority:
- the Sheriff for criminal matters; - the Station Representative for civil and administrative matters; - the highest-ranking NFSD officer if the Sheriff is unavailable; - the captain for ship-internal rules and private contracts.
12.2. Above them stands the SolGov Frontier Commissioner, the appointed SolGov authority for final review, extraordinary appeals, and matters beyond the Station Representative and Sheriff. (OOC: represented in-game by Central Command.)
12.3. Disputed cases and appeals are heard by a Frontier Tribunal. The Tribunal may be convened by the Station Representative, the Sheriff, or the accused. (OOC: player-run.)
12.4. The Tribunal may be composed of any available citizens. The presiding judge is the Station Representative, the Sheriff, or another citizen agreed by the parties. (OOC: no dedicated judge role is required.)
12.5. If a Tribunal cannot be formed, Central Command reviews the matter.
### Article 13 — Prosecution and Defense
13.1. The NFSD may prosecute criminal cases. In the absence of NFSD representatives or higher authority, the Station Representative may prosecute criminal cases. The Station Representative or another SolGov official may prosecute civil and administrative cases.
13.2. The accused may represent themselves or choose any available person as defense counsel. No legal license is required to serve as defense counsel.
13.3. A person may not serve as both prosecutor and judge in the same case.
13.4. If only one official is available, that official may detain the accused and refer the case to Central Command rather than judging it personally.
### Article 14 — Standard of Proof and Rights of the Accused
14.1. Every accused person is presumed innocent.
14.2. Guilt must be proven beyond a reasonable doubt.
14.3. The accused has the right to:
- remain silent; - know the charges; - examine the evidence against them; - present evidence and witnesses; - counsel or self-representation; - a prompt hearing; - freedom from double jeopardy; - appeal.
14.4. A confession obtained through torture, coercion, or unlawful mind control is inadmissible.
14.5. The accused has the right to necessary medical care while in custody.
### Article 15 — Warrants and Searches
15.1. Warrants are issued by the Station Representative or the Sheriff. If neither is available, the highest-ranking NFSD officer may authorize a warrant, with notification to Central Command.
15.2. A warrant is required for an extensive or fine-grained search, or for a targeted search of all of a person’s possessions, vessels, and property.
15.3. The NFSD may inspect cargo and board and search vessels without a warrant. This authority includes law-enforcement, customs, and safety inspections.
15.4. A search may proceed without a warrant where:
- the person with authority consents; - there is an immediate danger to life or limb; - evidence is about to be destroyed; - an officer is in hot pursuit; - customs or security inspection at an official port is authorized; - a vessel is being inspected for immediate safety reasons; - impounded property is being inventoried.
15.5. Searches of persons require probable cause. A protective pat-down for weapons is permitted during a lawful detention.
15.6. Seized property must be receipted. Contraband and evidence may be retained; lawful property must be returned when no longer needed.
15.7. NFSD should announce their presence before entering private premises unless doing so would endanger life or allow evidence to be destroyed.
### Article 16 — Arrest and Citizen’s Arrest
16.1. The NFSD may arrest a person on probable cause, on a warrant, or for an offense committed in their presence.
16.2. Any person may make a citizen’s arrest for an offense committed in their presence. The person must use only reasonable force and must promptly transfer the detainee to the NFSD.
16.3. A person making a citizen’s arrest is not immune from liability for excessive force or unlawful conduct.
16.4. Bounty hunters have no general police powers. They may use force only in self-defense or in a lawful citizen’s arrest, and must comply with NFSD authority.
16.5. A person may challenge an unlawful arrest before a tribunal, but may not use force against an officer solely because they believe the arrest is unlawful.
### Article 17 — Detention and Charges
17.1. A detainee must be informed of the charges promptly.
17.2. A detainee must be charged within 72 in-character hours. Medical and emergency time is excluded. (OOC: for gameplay, this ordinarily means before the end of the current shift unless NFSD command authorizes a logged extension; a detainee may cryo or change characters rather than wait.)
17.3. A detainee has the right to counsel, communication, medical care, food, water, and clothing.
17.4. If no charge is filed, the detainee must be released and lawful property returned.
17.5. The NFSD may hold a person in protective custody if they pose an imminent danger to themselves or others. Protective custody must be reviewed by the Station Representative or Sheriff.
### Article 18 — Appeals and Records
18.1. A disputed verdict or sentence may be appealed to the Station Representative or Sheriff.
18.2. A final appeal may be made to Central Command or SolGov officials.
18.3. Appeals may be heard summarily. Grounds include new evidence, procedural violation, excessive sentence, or bias.
18.4. Criminal records are public. Minor offenses may be expunged after a reasonable period set by the Penal Code. Sensitive records may be sealed by order of the Station Representative, Sheriff, or Central Command.
### Article 19 — Sentencing Authority
19.1. The highest available authority under Article 12 imposes sentence.
19.2. Sentences must be recorded, including the offense, the sentence, and the authority imposing it.
19.3. A sentence may be appealed under Article 18.
19.4. No summary execution is permitted. Execution requires the procedure in Article 52.
## Part IV — Offenses Against Persons
### Article 20 — Homicide
20.1. [bold]Murder[/bold] is an intentional or knowing unlawful killing.
20.2. [bold]Murder in the first degree[/bold] includes premeditated killing and killing committed during a serious felony such as robbery, kidnapping, piracy, terrorism, or sabotage.
20.3. [bold]Murder in the second degree[/bold] is an intentional killing without premeditation.
20.4. [bold]Manslaughter[/bold] is an unlawful killing without the intent or malice required for murder, including criminal recklessness or negligence.
20.5. [bold]Attempted murder[/bold] requires intent to kill and a substantial step toward doing so.
20.6. [bold]Prevention of revival[/bold] is a separate offense: deliberately rendering a body unresurrectable, hiding a body, or otherwise preventing revival.
20.7. A person may use force in self-defense or defense of another. Lethal force is justified only where the person reasonably believes it is necessary to prevent imminent death or serious bodily injury. Force used after the threat has ended is not self-defense.
20.8. A death caused during a serious felony may be charged as murder against a participant who caused or foreseeably contributed to the death.
### Article 21 — Assault, Threats, and Harassment
21.1. [bold]Assault[/bold] is unlawful physical force or a credible threat of imminent physical force.
21.2. [bold]Aggravated assault[/bold] includes assault with a weapon, assault causing serious injury, assault on an official, or assault on a vulnerable person.
21.3. [bold]Harassment[/bold] is repeated unwanted contact, threats, or conduct intended to intimidate, degrade, or alarm another person.
21.4. [bold]Sexual harassment[/bold] is unwanted sexual attention, comments, or conduct. It is a serious offense.
21.5. A person may use reasonable force to defend against an assault, subject to Article 20.7.
### Article 22 — Kidnapping and Unlawful Confinement
22.1. [bold]Kidnapping[/bold] is unlawfully restraining, transporting, controlling, or confining a person against their will.
22.2. [bold]Aggravated kidnapping[/bold] includes ransom, hostage-taking, serious injury, use of a weapon, or holding a public official.
22.3. Unlawful confinement includes detaining a person without lawful authority, even without moving them.
22.4. Hostage-taking is a serious offense and may be charged with kidnapping, terrorism, or both.
### Article 23 — Sexual Offenses
23.1. [bold]Public sexual activity[/bold] is prohibited in public places.
23.2. [bold]Sexual harassment[/bold] and [bold]non-consensual sexual conduct[/bold] are serious offenses.
23.3. [bold]Prostitution and solicitation[/bold] are prohibited. This includes offering, soliciting, brokering, or paying for sexual acts, and operating a brothel.
23.4. Private consensual sexual activity between adults is lawful in private places.
23.5. Consent must be informed and ongoing. A person may withdraw consent at any time.
### Article 24 — Animal Cruelty
24.1. [bold]Cruelty to animals[/bold] is prohibited. This includes unnecessary suffering or harm to any animal.
24.2. The following are not cruelty:
- killing animals for food; - pest control; - defense of a person or property from a dangerous animal; - veterinary care; - authorized research.
24.3. Owners are responsible for controlling dangerous animals.
### Article 25 — Reckless Endangerment and Negligence
25.1. [bold]Reckless endangerment[/bold] is conduct that creates a substantial and unjustifiable risk of death or serious bodily injury.
25.2. [bold]Criminal negligence[/bold] is a failure to exercise reasonable care that causes harm.
25.3. [bold]Professional negligence[/bold] by medical, engineering, or safety personnel may be a criminal offense, a civil matter, or both, and may result in license revocation.
25.4. Officials and crew with assigned safety duties have a duty to act within their training and authority.
## Part V — Property, Ships, and Commerce
### Article 26 — Theft and Property Offenses
26.1. [bold]Theft[/bold] is taking property without consent with intent to deprive the owner.
26.2. Theft is graded by value, operational importance, and replaceability. The Penal Code shall set the thresholds.
26.3. [bold]Petty theft[/bold] is low-value or replaceable property. [bold]Grand theft[/bold] is high-value, critical, or unreplaceable property.
26.4. Theft of SolGov, NFSD, or Frontier Administration property is an aggravating factor.
26.5. Theft of high-value strategic property may also constitute sabotage. Treason requires intent to aid an enemy; value alone is not enough.
26.6. [bold]Robbery[/bold] is theft by force or threat. [bold]Burglary[/bold] is unlawful entry with intent to commit a crime.
26.7. Fraud, embezzlement, extortion, and receiving stolen property are offenses.
26.8. A person who finds lost property must make a reasonable effort to return it. Keeping it without reasonable effort is theft.
26.9. [bold]Vandalism[/bold] and [bold]property damage[/bold] are offenses. Accidental damage is treated like a vehicle accident: civil liability and negligence may apply, but criminal intent is required for vandalism.
### Article 27 — Trespass
27.1. Unauthorized entry into private or restricted property is trespass.
27.2. Public areas are open to the public. Restricted areas must be marked or reasonably apparent.
27.3. Entry onto a private vessel requires the captain’s consent, a warrant, or an emergency.
27.4. Remaining in a place after being lawfully ordered to leave is trespass.
27.5. [bold]Aggravated trespass[/bold] includes entry into secure areas such as NFSD facilities, command areas, the vault, the armory, telecommunications, bridge, or engine rooms.
### Article 28 — Sabotage and Critical Infrastructure
28.1. [bold]Sabotage[/bold] is deliberate damage to, or interference with, critical infrastructure, including power, atmospherics, life support, navigation, communications, medical systems, security systems, or a vessel’s hull.
28.2. [bold]Mass destruction[/bold] is sabotage or violence that threatens to destroy or render uninhabitable a station, outpost, or vessel.
28.3. Sabotage of SolGov, NFSD, or Frontier Administration property is an aggravating factor.
28.4. Accidental damage is handled under Article 25.
### Article 29 — Ships, Deeds, and Salvage
29.1. The Bluespace Dock and Ship Registrar record vessel deeds. A deed is prima facie proof of ownership.
29.2. A vessel with no valid deed or registration is salvageable.
29.3. A vessel with a valid deed is not abandoned merely because it is unattended, docked, or open to the public. It may be treated as abandoned only if it has been left unpowered in space for more than four days. (OOC: this is difficult to prove in court.)
29.4. A salvor must make reasonable efforts to contact the owner before taking possession.
29.5. Cargo follows the vessel unless it is separately abandoned or owned.
29.6. A forged deed is void and is a criminal offense.
29.7. The NFSD may impound a vessel used in a crime or posing an immediate danger. Impoundment must be recorded and may be appealed.
### Article 30 — Construction and Claims
30.1. Construction and continued use establish a prima facie claim to property. No paperwork is required.
30.2. The Frontier Administration may keep records of claims for convenience. The absence of a record does not defeat a good-faith claim. (OOC: admin logs may be used as evidence in a dispute.)
30.3. Disputes over construction, mining, or occupied property are heard by a tribunal.
### Article 31 — Customs, Tariffs, Smuggling, and Quarantine
31.1. Tariffs and docking taxes are administered through the Bluespace Dock and cargo systems.
31.2. The NFSD may inspect cargo at official stations and outposts, and aboard vessels, without a warrant for law-enforcement, customs, or safety purposes.
31.3. [bold]Smuggling[/bold] is concealing cargo or contraband from a lawful inspection or evading tariffs.
31.4. Trade with a hostile power or organization is prohibited.
31.5. Quarantine orders are enforceable. Violation is an offense.
### Article 32 — Gambling
32.1. Gambling is lawful when licensed by the Frontier Administration.
32.2. Fraud, rigged games, and coercion to collect gambling debts are offenses.
32.3. Unlicensed gambling may be shut down and fined.
### Article 33 — Corporate and Economic Offenses
33.1. Corporations are legal persons. They may be fined, sanctioned, or dissolved. Directing officers may be personally liable.
33.2. Fraud, forgery, counterfeiting, impersonation, bribery, extortion, embezzlement, money laundering, and abuse of public office are offenses.
33.3. Impersonating SolGov, NFSD, or Frontier Administration officials is an aggravated offense.
33.4. Corporate espionage, trade-secret theft, and sabotage are offenses.
### Article 34 — Intellectual Property
34.1. Patents, trademarks, and copyright are primarily civil matters.
34.2. Trade-secret theft, sabotage, and corporate espionage are criminal.
34.3. Counterfeit goods may be seized as contraband.
## Part VI — Public Order and Safety
### Article 35 — Public Conduct and Nudity
35.1. Nudity is prohibited in public places.
35.2. Nudity is permitted in private places, including private quarters, dormitories, bathrooms, and private vessels.
35.3. A private vessel is a private place. A captain may permit nudity aboard their vessel.
35.4. A vessel remains a private place even if its captain opens it to the public. Everyone entering a vessel is understood to have agreed to the captain’s rules.
35.5. Public sexual activity is prohibited under Article 23.
### Article 36 — Controlled Substances and Alcohol
36.1. Alcohol is lawful with a license. Public intoxication is an offense.
36.2. A substance is illegal if it causes harm to persons other than the user, or if it can be weaponized. A substance that harms only the person consuming it is legal.
36.3. Substances that harm others through smoke, vapor, area effects, secondhand exposure, or persistent discomfort are illegal.
36.4. Cannabis is legal but must be consumed privately. Public consumption is an offense. Smoke and odor are transmission vectors and may support additional charges, including pollution.
36.5. Possession, use, distribution, and manufacture may be separate offenses.
36.6. Piloting a vessel while intoxicated is an aggravated offense.
### Article 37 — Weapons and Contraband
37.1. Contraband is divided into five tiers under Appendix A.
37.2. Tier 1 through Tier 4 items require a permit. Tier 5 is not available by permit; possession is restricted to the TSF military, the NFSD, and authorized SolGov officials acting in the course of their duties.
37.3. Enforcement priorities:
- Tier 1 and Tier 2: permit required, but generally low priority absent another offense. - Tier 3: permit required; NFSD may investigate and seize. - Tier 4: permit required; unauthorized possession is arrestable. - Tier 5: military and law-enforcement hardware; unauthorized possession is a serious offense.
37.4. Permits are issued by the Station Representative or Sheriff and may require training or registration.
37.5. Brandishing a weapon, threatening with a weapon, or discharging a weapon in public is an offense.
37.6. Self-defense with a weapon is governed by Article 20.7.
37.7. Explosives and weapons of mass destruction are heavily restricted under Article 43.
37.8. The NFSD is a law-enforcement agency with military-grade equipment. It is not a branch or reserve component of the military.
### Article 38 — Traffic and Piloting
38.1. SolGov traffic rules apply in the Frontier Sector.
38.2. Reckless piloting, hit-and-run, false distress calls, and no-fly-zone violations are offenses.
38.3. A no-fly zone must be publicly announced and clearly defined before enforcement. A vessel that violates a declared no-fly zone may be treated as an active hostile unidentified combatant and engaged with lethal force.
38.4. Blockades may be established only by the NFSD or SolGov authority. Private blockades are unlawful.
38.5. Piloting under the influence is an aggravated offense.
38.6. Vessels must obey lawful traffic-control instructions.
### Article 39 — Public Health
39.1. The Station Representative or Sheriff may impose quarantine for a dangerous communicable disease.
39.2. Bioweapons are illegal.
39.3. A person who knows they carry a dangerous communicable disease must report it to medical authorities.
39.4. Medical privacy is protected, with a public-safety exception.
39.5. Refusing a lawful quarantine or medical examination is an offense.
### Article 40 — Environment
40.1. Pollution, toxic waste dumping, and unsafe radiation release are offenses.
40.2. Industrial discharge requires a permit.
40.3. Terraforming and large-scale environmental modification are regulated by the Frontier Administration.
40.4. Poaching protected wildlife is an offense. Hunting for food is lawful.
## Part VII — Security and Foreign Relations
### Article 41 — Piracy, Privateering, and Mercenaries
41.1. [bold]Piracy[/bold] is the unauthorized robbery, hostile boarding, seizure, or hijacking of a vessel or its cargo through force, threats, or coercion.
41.2. [bold]Privateering[/bold] is lawful only under a letter of marque issued by SolGov. Without one, it is piracy.
41.3. [bold]Mercenaries[/bold] may operate under a lawful contract and license. They remain subject to the Code and have no general police powers.
41.4. [bold]Bounty hunters[/bold] may operate under a license. They should capture rather than kill where reasonably possible. Lethal force is permitted only in self-defense or defense of another.
41.5. Ransom and hostage-taking are illegal.
41.6. False flags used to commit piracy or treason are an aggravating factor.
### Article 42 — Treason, Sedition, and Espionage
42.1. [bold]Treason[/bold] requires intentional aid to an enemy or hostile foreign power, or an attempt to overthrow SolGov by force.
42.2. [bold]Sedition[/bold] requires incitement to violence or overthrow. Criticism of the government is not sedition.
42.3. [bold]Espionage[/bold] requires the unauthorized acquisition or disclosure of classified SolGov information.
42.4. Impersonating a SolGov official is an offense.
### Article 43 — Terrorism and Mass Destruction
43.1. [bold]Terrorism[/bold] is violence or property destruction intended to intimidate the government or civilians, or to coerce policy.
43.2. [bold]Mass destruction[/bold] includes weapons of mass destruction, station-wide destruction, and attacks causing mass casualties.
43.3. Weapons of mass destruction are illegal except when authorized by SolGov.
43.4. False bomb threats and false weapons-of-mass-destruction reports are serious offenses.
### Article 44 — War Crimes and Prisoners of War
44.1. This Article applies during a declared armed conflict.
44.2. Civilians must not be deliberately targeted.
44.3. Prisoners of war must receive humane treatment, medical care, food, water, and protection from violence.
44.4. Torture, summary execution, and collective punishment are prohibited.
44.5. War crimes are prosecuted by SolGov or a tribunal.
## Part VIII — Status and Liability
### Article 45 — Synths, Silicons, and AI
45.1. A Synth is a sentient person and is liable for their own conduct.
45.2. A lawed Silicon is not independently liable for an offense. Liability falls on the programmer, owner, or person who gave the unlawful order.
45.3. Unlawfully modifying a Silicon’s laws is an offense.
45.4. Destroying a lawed Silicon may be prosecuted as property damage. Destroying a Synth may be prosecuted as assault or homicide.
45.5. A lawed Silicon is the property of its registered owner unless SolGov grants it legal personhood.
### Article 46 — Clones, Revival, and Mind Control
46.1. A clone or revived person is the same legal person as before revival. They retain identity, rights, and obligations.
46.2. Mind control is illegal. A person acting under unlawful mind control is not culpable if they lacked control.
46.3. The controller and anyone who knowingly enabled the control are liable.
46.4. Prevention of revival is a separate offense under Article 20.6.
46.5. Unauthorized removal of organs from a living or deceased person is an offense.
### Article 47 — Corporations and Public Officials
47.1. Corporations are legal persons and may be held liable.
47.2. Bribery, corruption, abuse of office, conflict of interest, and disclosure of confidential information are offenses.
47.3. Public officials are subject to the Code. No immunity is recognized.
47.4. Good-faith reports of official misconduct are protected.
## OOC Disclaimer
This page is in-character law. It does not replace the server rules. Certain offenses described here may also be violations of the server rules and may result in staff punishment, including bans.
